title: Design: Count* aggregate methods on storage.Storage
description:
Parent architecture: be-yinl4d.

# Goal

Add aggregate `Count*` methods to `storage.Storage` so that callers needing only cardinality (`len(issues) > 0`, hub-bead progress, etc.) skip the row materialization entirely.

# Architect-fixed decisions

- **Methods to add:** CountIssues, CountDependents, CountDependencies, CountIssueComments, CountEvents.
- **Implementation:** direct `SELECT count(*) FROM <table> WHERE <filter>` on both backends. REUSE the canonical filter builder `internal/storage/issueops/filters.go::BuildIssueFilterClauses`; only the projection changes.
- **Return type:** int64 (not int) — match SQL COUNT(*) semantics; future-proofs against >2B rows.
- **No new SQL infrastructure needed.** PG side already has the `add()` placeholder helper.

# What the designer must produce

1. Method signatures on storage.Storage (and DependencyQueryStore where applicable).
2. PG implementations in internal/storage/postgres/ that mirror the existing filter EXISTS pattern (reuse from queries.go:40-53 for label EXISTS).
3. Dolt implementations using the canonical filter builder.
4. Parity tests in internal/storage/parity/ covering each Count method against fixtures with: empty result set, single match, label-filter-narrowing, parent filter.
5. Confirm O(log N) or better against a 100K-row fixture (bench), so the migration to Count from len(SearchIssues) is unambiguously a win.

# Coverage of CLI call sites (NOT migrated in this bead — separate bead)

The following will eventually call Count* (tracked in a follow-up CLI-migration bead):
- bd info --hub-counts
- bd preflight
- bd close epic-closure check
- bd ping

# Out of scope

- CLI migrations (separate bead).
- Iter* methods (separate bead).

# Done-when

- All five Count* methods exist on storage.Storage.
- Parity tests pass under `go test -tags 'gms_pure_go integration_pg' ./internal/storage/parity/...`
- A new BenchmarkCountIssuesVsLen demonstrates Count* is at least 50x faster than `len(SearchIssues(...))` on a 10K-row fixture.
- `go build -tags gms_pure_go ./...` clean.

# Note from architect

This is a small bead; resist the temptation to also migrate CLI callers in the same PR. Keep this PR focused on the storage layer.
close_reason:
Design complete (per designer 2026-05-07). Decomposed into:
- be-74hkw2 (precursor: extract buildSearchClause helper, shared with be-jaavsb plan)
- be-fv0xme (impl: Count* aggregate methods on storage.Storage, single PR per designer)

be-fv0xme blocks be-pkg36q (CLI count migrations). Plan: docs/plans/be-rqyhbb-count-aggregates.md

title: Design: Iter[T] interface + Iter* methods on storage.Storage (shape only)
description:
Parent architecture: be-yinl4d.

# Goal

Introduce `storage.Iter[T any]` (Next/Value/Err/Close) as the canonical streaming-iterator shape and add `Iter*` siblings to every method on `storage.Storage` that today returns a potentially unbounded slice. NO CLI migrations in this bead — interface and skeleton implementations only.

# Architect-fixed decisions (do not redo)

- **Iterator shape:** generic `Iter[T]` with Next(ctx)/Value()/Err()/Close(). Do NOT introduce per-type iterators (no `IssueIter`, `EventIter`).
- **Local impl:** thin wrapper around `*sql.Rows` (Dolt) or `pgx.Rows` (PG). NO goroutines, NO buffered channels — pure pull-based.
- **Per-row hydration must use a dedicated connection.** PG iterator MUST hold its own pool connection for the iterator's lifetime.
- **No new vendored deps.** stdlib + already-vendored modules only.
- **RPC transport NOT in this bead.** Iterator over RPC depends on be-oyer9z (bdd daemon); ship in-process iterators first.

# Methods to add (full list — see be-yinl4d §8)

- IterIssues, IterDependentsWithMetadata, IterDependenciesWithMetadata, IterIssueComments, IterEvents, IterAllEventsSince, IterReadyWork, IterBlockedIssues, IterWisps, plus IterAllDependencyRecords on DependencyQueryStore.

# What the designer must produce

1. The exact `Iter[T]` interface signature including doc comment.
2. PG and Dolt skeleton implementations for at least IterIssues + IterDependentsWithMetadata. The other Iter methods can stub-call the slice version internally (and TODO the streaming impl in follow-up beads). The Iter SHAPE and skeleton matters most here — the per-method optimizations come later.
3. Parity tests in `internal/storage/parity/` covering Iter happy path + Close-during-iteration + sentinel error round-trip on Err().
4. Audit which existing fields/types are not gob-friendly (relevant for be-oyer9z later) — flag any maps with non-string keys, channels, function pointers in the iterated types.
5. ForEachIssue helper (see be-yinl4d §13) as a convenience for tests / simple callers.

# Out of scope

- CLI migrations (separate beads — see be-yinl4d §18 items 3–8).
- Count* methods (separate bead).
- Daemon RPC iterators (depends on be-oyer9z).
- Streaming JSON output in cmd/bd (separate beads).

# Done-when

- `storage.Iter[T]` interface lands with full doc comment.
- All Iter* methods exist on storage.Storage (some skeleton-only is OK).
- IterIssues + IterDependentsWithMetadata are fully streaming on both PG and Dolt.
- Parity tests pass under `go test -tags 'gms_pure_go integration_pg' ./internal/storage/parity/...`
- `go build -tags gms_pure_go ./...` clean.
- `golangci-lint run --build-tags=gms_pure_go ./internal/storage/...` clean (or matches LINTING.md baseline).
close_reason:
Design complete (per designer 2026-05-07). Decomposed into:
- be-74hkw2 (precursor: extract buildSearchClause helper)
- be-u0zlsq (impl: Iter[T] interface + Iter* methods, single PR per designer)

be-u0zlsq blocks be-c40q2v / be-775o60 / be-7hvi6c / be-f68axd / be-60kmhm and unblocks be-oyer9z. Plan: docs/plans/be-jaavsb-iter-interface.md

title: [postgres] dsn.ConfigToConnString silently promotes sslmode prefer/allow/verify-* → require on round-trip
description: Discovered while writing tests for be-0d4.
notes:
## Symptom

`internal/storage/postgres/dsn/strip.go:ConfigToConnString` cannot
faithfully round-trip soft sslmode values. Empirical pgconn probe:

  input        runtime[sslmode]   tls_nil   round-trip output
  disable      not present        true      sslmode=disable   ✓
  allow        not present        true      sslmode=disable   ✗ (downgrade)
  prefer       not present        false     sslmode=require   ✗ (silent promotion — the case in the be-0d4 bead)
  require      not present        false     sslmode=require   ✓
  verify-ca    not present        false     sslmode=require   ✗ (drops cert verification)
  verify-full  not present        false     sslmode=require   ✗ (drops cert verification)

pgx/v5 (pgconn.ParseConfig) collapses every sslmode into *tls.Config and
removes it from RuntimeParams. The current ConfigToConnString fallback
chooses between `disable` (TLSConfig nil) and `require` (TLSConfig non-nil)
— it has no way to recover the original sslmode string from cfg alone.

## Reach

Persists to metadata.json on every PG-backed `bd init`. Operationally:

- Operators who set `sslmode=prefer` (PG default for many cloud setups)
  end up with `sslmode=require` saved to disk after the first round-trip,
  silently changing connection-establishment behavior.
- Operators using cert-pinning (`verify-ca`/`verify-full`) get downgraded
  to `require`, which negotiates TLS but does not verify the server cert.
  This is the security-relevant case.

## Why this slipped through

The existing `TestComposeRoundTrip` in
`internal/storage/postgres/dsn/strip_test.go` only exercises `sslmode=require`,
where round-trip happens to be lossless because the fallback emits `require`.
be-0d4's "tightening alongside" item asks for a soft-sslmode round-trip test;
that test would fail today, which is how I caught this.

## Fix sketch

ConfigToConnString cannot recover the original sslmode from cfg.
Options:

1. **Don't go through pgconn for the round-trip.** Strip can preserve the
   original DSN by parsing the URL/keyword form ourselves, surgically
   removing the password, and emitting the result verbatim. pgconn would
   still validate, but the persisted form would be the input's own
   sslmode/host/db/etc. fields. Lower-effort, removes the lossy
   approximation entirely.

2. **Side-channel the original sslmode.** Strip stores the original
   sslmode separately and Compose puts it back. Coordinates with the
   round-trip logic in ConfigToConnString. More moving parts.

Option 1 is preferable.

## Acceptance

- Round-trip preserves sslmode for {disable, allow, prefer, require,
  verify-ca, verify-full}.
- `TestComposeRoundTripPreservesSoftSSLMode` (or similar) added to
  `internal/storage/postgres/dsn/strip_test.go` asserting the invariant.
- Existing TestStrip / TestComposeRoundTrip remain passing.

## Related

- Discovered while writing tests for be-0d4 (see notes there).
- Source code: internal/storage/postgres/dsn/strip.go:61-105.

## Tests written (validator handoff)

Branch: tests/be-g4x0eq-sslmode-roundtrip (off local-integ @ a67427829)
Commit: 1bfce9131 — test(postgres/dsn): be-g4x0eq pin sslmode round-trip invariant (failing)

File: internal/storage/postgres/dsn/strip_test.go (added one test func with
6 sub-cases — no build tag; pure-Go test)

Coverage: TestComposeRoundTripPreservesSoftSSLMode iterates over the six
libpq sslmode values {disable, allow, prefer, require, verify-ca, verify-full}.
For each input, runs Strip → Compose and asserts:
  - The input's sslmode appears in BOTH the stripped and composed output
  - No OTHER sslmode value appears (catches silent substitution)

Both stages are probed because they share ConfigToConnString, so the
failure log distinguishes promotion vs downgrade vs drop.

## Failing subtests today

  PASS  disable    (TLSConfig nil → emits disable)
  FAIL  allow      → silently downgrades to disable
  FAIL  prefer     → silently promotes to require
  PASS  require    (TLSConfig non-nil → emits require)
  FAIL  verify-ca  → silently downgrades to require (drops cert verification!)
  FAIL  verify-full → silently downgrades to require (drops cert verification!)

The verify-ca / verify-full cases are the security-relevant ones —
silently degrading from cert-pinned TLS to "require" is a quiet
weakening of the operator's intent.

## Implementation hint (recommended fix path)

ConfigToConnString cannot recover the original sslmode from cfg because
pgconn.ParseConfig collapses all sslmode values into *tls.Config and
removes them from RuntimeParams.

Recommended approach: skip the pgconn round-trip entirely for the
strip/compose path. Parse the URL/keyword form ourselves, surgically
remove (or inject) the password component, and emit verbatim. pgconn
can still validate up-front (the existing call inside Strip), but the
serialized form should be the operator's input verbatim minus the
password.

Touchpoints:
- internal/storage/postgres/dsn/strip.go:Strip — currently
  cfg.Password = "" + ConfigToConnString. Replace with textual edit.
- internal/storage/postgres/dsn/strip.go:Compose — currently
  cfg.Password = password + ConfigToConnString. Replace with textual
  edit that injects password into the user portion of the URL (or
  password=... in keyword form).
- ConfigToConnString itself can stay (some other call site may use it),
  but the lossy fallback comment should be updated.

Run after the fix:
  go test -tags 'gms_pure_go' -run \
    'TestStrip|TestCompose|TestComposeRoundTripPreservesSoftSSLMode' \
    ./internal/storage/postgres/dsn/
  → all sub-cases must PASS.
close_reason: Fixed: Strip/Compose now preserve operator's sslmode on round-trip. URI-form inputs go through net/url for textual password edit (everything else verbatim). Keyword-form inputs recover sslmode from raw text and stuff into cfg.RuntimeParams before ConfigToConnString. All 6 sub-cases of TestComposeRoundTripPreservesSoftSSLMode pass; full ./internal/storage/postgres/... green; lint 0 issues. Commit 040352a50 on fix/be-g4x0eq. Routing to reviewer.

title: Architecture: streaming storage interface — bound bd RAM by pushing aggregates/iteration to SQL
description:
# Architecture — Streaming storage interface to bound bd RAM

**Bead:** be-yinl4d · **Author:** beads/architect · **Date:** 2026-05-07
**Predecessors:** be-4d36f2 (RAM bug, hot fix landed in PR #3768) · be-szr (related fix b8c4a83c0) · be-jdeief (PG SearchIssues filter coverage gap; parallel)
**Related (downstream):** be-ef3q3u (cold-start RAM budget; this work composes with the daemon proposal) · be-oyer9z (bdd daemon design — iterator transport must work over net/rpc + gob)
**Cross-rig (out of scope here):** be-aw0afh (gc nudge drain subprocess storm — gc-management side)

---

## 1. Problem

`bd` materializes full result sets in Go memory before writing output, even when the SQL backend could stream / aggregate / paginate the answer. PR #3768 patched the most-common cliff (`bd show --json` allocating 5–13 GB on hub beads with thousands of dependents), but the underlying pattern remains:

- **Triple materialization.** Storage methods like `Storage.GetDependentsWithMetadata`, `Storage.GetIssueComments`, `Storage.GetEvents`, `Storage.SearchIssues` return `[]*types.X`. The CLI then JSON-marshals the slice. For unbounded result sets the full set lives in Go memory once during fetch, again during marshaling, and a third time inside `encoding/json`'s reflect-based walk. On hub beads or `--limit 0` queries this multiplies into GBs.
- **Cardinality queries pay full freight.** Several call sites only need a count (`len(issues)`), but the implementation pulls every row, hydrates labels, allocates structs, then discards everything but the length. Both PG (`SELECT count(*)`) and Dolt know the answer cheaply.
- **Both backends already speak streaming** at the engine layer — `pgx.Rows.Next()` for PG, `sql.Rows.Next()` against the Dolt SQL engine — but the Storage interface forces bulk materialization regardless.

## 2. Decision

Adopt **option 4 from be-yinl4d** — a layered combination — with the specifics below. None of the four candidate shapes is right alone:

| Shape | Verdict | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **(1) Iterator interface** | **Adopt for unbounded slices.** | Canonical Go pattern; works cleanly over both backends and over RPC via batch+cursor. |
| **(2) Streaming JSON writer on Storage** | **Reject.** | Creates a parallel API surface — every caller wanting filtering, formatting, transforms, or pagination duplicates logic into both the slice and the writer path. Storage stays "pure data"; CLI handles JSON streaming. |
| **(3) Aggregate methods** | **Adopt for cardinality.** | Easiest, highest-leverage win. SQL `COUNT(*)` is O(1)–O(log N) instead of O(N) of materialized rows. |
| **(4) Combination** | **The actual answer.** | Iterator + counts + retained slice for *bounded* queries. Most call sites stay unchanged. |

The detailed contract is §6–§9 below.

## 3. Requirements

### Functional

- **FR-01** A new public method shape `Iter*(ctx, ...) (Iter[T], error)` SHALL exist on `storage.Storage` for every method listed in §4 *Affected surface*, returning a streaming iterator instead of a materialized slice.
- **FR-02** A new public method shape `Count*(ctx, ...) (int64, error)` SHALL exist for the cardinality-only call sites listed in §4.
- **FR-03** The existing slice-returning methods (`SearchIssues`, `GetDependentsWithMetadata`, `GetIssueComments`, `GetEvents`, etc.) SHALL be retained for bounded callers — typically those passing `IssueFilter.Limit > 0` or otherwise structurally bounded (e.g., `GetIssue`, single-bead reads). They are **not deprecated**, but the slice path SHALL refuse `--limit 0` (unbounded) and route via the iterator instead. Rationale in §13.
- **FR-04** CLI commands listed in §5 *CLI migration* SHALL switch to `Count*` for cardinality questions and to `Iter*` for unbounded JSON output.
- **FR-05** Iterator return shape MUST be transport-agnostic — the same `Iter[T]` interface SHALL satisfy both the in-process Storage backend and the daemon RPC client (be-oyer9z), using server-side batching with a cursor token for the RPC path. See §6.
- **FR-06** `errors.Is` MUST behave the same on iterators as on slice methods. Sentinel errors (`storage.ErrNotFound`, `storage.ErrPrefixMismatch`, etc.) SHALL surface from `Iter.Err()` after `Iter.Next()` returns false.
- **FR-07** Iterator close-on-cancel MUST release backend resources (release cursor on PG, close `sql.Rows` on Dolt, send `IterClose` on RPC). Failing to call `Close()` MUST not leak goroutines or DB cursors past context cancellation.
- **FR-08** Both backends (PG and Dolt) MUST implement the iterator and aggregate methods; `internal/storage/parity/` SHALL exercise both transports.

### Non-functional

- **NFR-01 (RAM)** Steady-state RSS for `bd show --json <hub-bead>` (10K dependents) MUST land below **50 MB** end-to-end with the streaming pipeline (down from 5–13 GB pre-PR #3768; PR #3768 caps the ceiling but only by stripping fields). Steady-state RSS for `bd list --label X --include-* --limit 0` on a 152-row dataset MUST land below **20 MB** (down from 13 GB).
- **NFR-02 (latency)** Hot-path single-row read MUST not regress more than 5% versus the in-process slice path on bounded queries (`--limit 50`). Iterator overhead is acceptable for unbounded queries where the slice path would OOM.
- **NFR-03 (transparency)** No user-visible CLI output change. JSON shape stays identical (array of objects); only the producer changes.
- **NFR-04 (RPC parity)** Iterator over net/rpc + gob (be-oyer9z transport) MUST round-trip with sentinel errors preserved. Default RPC batch size 100 rows; configurable via `daemon_iter_batch` metadata field.
- **NFR-05 (testability)** Parity tests in `internal/storage/parity/` MUST cover Count and Iter methods on both PG and Dolt. A new bench `BenchmarkSearchIssuesIter` SHALL pin the RAM ceiling for unbounded queries.
- **NFR-06 (rollback)** All iterator/count code paths gated behind feature work that doesn't change existing slice-method behavior. If a regression appears, callers can revert to the slice path with a one-line change.
- **NFR-07 (concurrency)** Multiple iterators on the same Storage handle MUST not deadlock. PG implementation uses a fresh connection per cursor; Dolt uses a fresh `sql.Rows` per iterator (already concurrency-safe per the `gms_pure_go` engine).

## 4. Constraints

| Type | Constraint | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Technical | Both backends must be supported. PG already has `pgx.Conn.Query` / `Rows.Next()`; Dolt has `sql.Rows`. The iterator implementation is a thin wrapper around each. | `internal/storage/postgres/`, `internal/storage/dolt/` |
| Technical | Daemon transport (be-oyer9z) is **net/rpc + gob over Unix socket**, *not* a streaming RPC. Iterator MUST therefore use server-side state (cursor token) and client-side batching, NOT an RPC stream. | be-ef3q3u §4 (transport choice frozen there); be-oyer9z A2/A3 |
| Technical | Sentinel error identity must round-trip over gob (NFR-05 from be-ef3q3u). The iterator's `Err()` channel uses the same envelope as slice methods. | NFR-05 (be-ef3q3u) |
| Technical | `IssueFilter.Limit` is the existing knob for bounded vs unbounded. We reuse it as the contract: `Limit > 0` ⇒ slice path is fine, `Limit == 0` (or large) ⇒ iterator path. No new filter field. | `internal/types/types.go:1203` |
| Technical | The PG `SearchIssues` filter coverage gap (be-jdeief) is parallel work — iterator inherits whatever WHERE clauses the slice path has at any given commit. Land the iterator on top of, not before, the be-jdeief fix when both touch `internal/storage/postgres/issues.go`. | be-jdeief |
| Technical | Existing tests use `SearchIssues(ctx, "", IssueFilter{})` to read all issues. Migrating tests to the iterator path is mechanical but bulk-touches; provide a `CollectIssues(iter)` helper to keep test code terse. | `cmd/bd/*_test.go` |
| Technical | Prior architecture (be-ef3q3u §4) chose `net/rpc + gob` to avoid new deps. Iterator design MUST stay within stdlib — no new vendored modules. | be-ef3q3u §4 |
| Operational | Parity-test suite is the authoritative cross-backend checker. Adding methods means extending it once, not per-backend. | `internal/storage/parity/` |
| Business | Hot fix in PR #3768 unblocks the immediate cliff; this architecture is the durable fix. No urgency that overrides design quality, but it should land before the next major hub-bead RAM regression. | be-yinl4d intake |

## 5. Library / framework selections

| Layer | Choice | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Iterator interface | **Generic** `Iter[T any] interface { Next(ctx) bool; Value() *T; Err() error; Close() error }` (Go 1.21+ generics) | One iterator type for issues, comments, events, dependents. Avoids per-type boilerplate. Mirrors `database/sql.Rows` shape. |
| Iterator local impl | Struct wrapping `*sql.Rows` (or `pgx.Rows`) + per-row scan func | Already concurrency-safe per the underlying driver. No goroutines, no buffered channels — pure pull-based. |
| Iterator RPC impl | Cursor-token + batch fetch over net/rpc | Server keeps an iterator session keyed by token; client prefetches N rows per `IterNext` call; `IterClose` releases. Idle iterators expire after 30 s server-side. |
| Aggregate impl | Direct SQL `COUNT(*)` with shared filter clauses (Dolt uses `BuildIssueFilterClauses` from `issueops/filters.go`; PG mirrors it) | The PG side already has `add()` placeholder helper; the Dolt side has the canonical filter builder. No new SQL infrastructure needed. |
| JSON streaming on CLI | Manual `[`/`,`/`]` framing + `json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(item)` per row | stdlib only. Encoder.Encode writes one object + newline; we trim the newline or leave it (jq-friendly either way). No new deps. |

**Net new dependencies: zero.** All work uses stdlib + existing helpers.

## 6. Iterator interface contract

```go
// Iter is a generic streaming iterator over a backend result set.
// Iter is single-pass and not safe for concurrent use.
//
// Usage:
//   it, err := store.IterIssues(ctx, query, filter)
//   if err != nil { return err }
//   defer it.Close()
//   for it.Next(ctx) {
//       issue := it.Value()
//       // ... use issue ...
//   }
//   if err := it.Err(); err != nil { return err }
type Iter[T any] interface {
    // Next advances the iterator. Returns true if a value is available
    // via Value(). Returns false on end-of-results OR on error; in the
    // error case, Err() returns the error.
    Next(ctx context.Context) bool

    // Value returns the row at the current cursor. Only valid after
    // Next() returns true. Returned pointer MAY be reused on the next
    // Next() call — callers that need to retain it across iterations
    // must copy.
    Value() *T

    // Err returns the first error encountered during iteration, or
    // nil if the iterator was exhausted cleanly.
    Err() error

    // Close releases backend resources (DB cursor, RPC session,
    // goroutines). Idempotent. Always safe to call.
    Close() error
}
```

**Local backend impl** (`internal/storage/postgres/issues.go`, `internal/storage/dolt/issues.go`):

```go
type pgIssueIter struct {
    rows *pgx.Rows
    cur  *types.Issue
    err  error
    s    *PostgresStore  // for hydrating labels / metadata per row
}

func (it *pgIssueIter) Next(ctx context.Context) bool {
    if it.err != nil { return false }
    if !it.rows.Next() { it.err = it.rows.Err(); return false }
    iss, err := scanIssueRow(it.rows)
    if err != nil { it.err = err; return false }
    if err := it.s.hydrateLabelsForIssue(ctx, iss); err != nil { it.err = err; return false }
    it.cur = iss
    return true
}
func (it *pgIssueIter) Value() *types.Issue { return it.cur }
func (it *pgIssueIter) Err() error { return it.err }
func (it *pgIssueIter) Close() error { return it.rows.Close() }
```

**Daemon RPC impl** (added in be-oyer9z follow-up):

```go
type rpcIssueIter struct {
    client    *rpc.Client
    sessionID string
    buf       []*types.Issue   // prefetched batch
    bufIdx    int
    done      bool
    err       error
}

func (it *rpcIssueIter) Next(ctx context.Context) bool {
    if it.err != nil || it.done { return false }
    if it.bufIdx >= len(it.buf) {
        var resp IterNextResp
        if err := it.client.Call("Storage.IterNext",
            IterNextReq{SessionID: it.sessionID, BatchSize: 100}, &resp); err != nil {
            it.err = decodeRPCError(err)
            return false
        }
        it.buf = resp.Items
        it.bufIdx = 0
        if resp.Done { it.done = true }
        if len(it.buf) == 0 { return false }
    }
    it.bufIdx++
    return true
}
func (it *rpcIssueIter) Value() *types.Issue { return it.buf[it.bufIdx-1] }
func (it *rpcIssueIter) Close() error {
    return it.client.Call("Storage.IterClose", IterCloseReq{SessionID: it.sessionID}, nil)
}
```

**RPC server side** (daemon in be-oyer9z):

- `IterStart(req IterStartReq) → (sessionID, err)` — opens a backend iterator, stashes it in a sessionID-keyed map, returns the token.
- `IterNext(req IterNextReq) → (items, done, err)` — drains up to BatchSize rows from the stashed iterator. Sets `done=true` when the underlying iterator is exhausted.
- `IterClose(req IterCloseReq) → err` — releases the stashed iterator.
- Idle reaper goroutine — closes any session with no recent activity (default 30 s). Prevents leaks on client crashes.

Server keeps O(active iterators) state; default cap **64 concurrent iterators per daemon**. `IterStart` returns `ErrTooManyIterators` if exceeded; client falls back to slice path with a warning. Cap is configurable via `daemon_iter_max` metadata field.

**Sentinel error round-trip:** the same envelope used for slice methods (`{kind, msg}` reconstructed via `decodeRPCError` — see be-oyer9z A2). `errors.Is(it.Err(), storage.ErrNotFound)` MUST behave identically across in-process and RPC.

## 7. Aggregate (count) interface contract

```go
// Added to storage.Storage:
CountIssues(ctx context.Context, query string, filter types.IssueFilter) (int64, error)
CountDependents(ctx context.Context, issueID string) (int64, error)
CountDependencies(ctx context.Context, issueID string) (int64, error)
CountIssueComments(ctx context.Context, issueID string) (int64, error)
CountEvents(ctx context.Context, issueID string) (int64, error)
```

Each is a direct `SELECT count(*) FROM <table> WHERE <filter>` — **no row materialization**. Both backends already share the WHERE-clause builder (`internal/storage/issueops/filters.go::BuildIssueFilterClauses`); aggregates reuse the same builder, only changing the `SELECT count(*)` projection.

Cost: O(1) for indexed counts (the index on `issues(status)` covers most filter shapes), O(log N) for filtered counts. Memory: ~negligible (one int64).

## 8. Storage interface — new methods (full list)

Added to `storage.Storage`:

```go
// Iterator variants — one per slice method that can return unbounded results.
IterIssues(ctx context.Context, query string, filter types.IssueFilter) (Iter[types.Issue], error)
IterDependentsWithMetadata(ctx context.Context, issueID string) (Iter[types.IssueWithDependencyMetadata], error)
IterDependenciesWithMetadata(ctx context.Context, issueID string) (Iter[types.IssueWithDependencyMetadata], error)
IterIssueComments(ctx context.Context, issueID string) (Iter[types.Comment], error)
IterEvents(ctx context.Context, issueID string, limit int) (Iter[types.Event], error)
IterAllEventsSince(ctx context.Context, since time.Time) (Iter[types.Event], error)
IterReadyWork(ctx context.Context, filter types.WorkFilter) (Iter[types.Issue], error)
IterBlockedIssues(ctx context.Context, filter types.WorkFilter) (Iter[types.BlockedIssue], error)
IterWisps(ctx context.Context, filter types.WispFilter) (Iter[types.Issue], error)

// Aggregates — one per count-only call site.
CountIssues(ctx context.Context, query string, filter types.IssueFilter) (int64, error)
CountDependents(ctx context.Context, issueID string) (int64, error)
CountDependencies(ctx context.Context, issueID string) (int64, error)
CountIssueComments(ctx context.Context, issueID string) (int64, error)
CountEvents(ctx context.Context, issueID string) (int64, error)
```

Existing slice-returning methods remain unchanged. Callers MAY use either; CLI migrations are documented in §9.

The DependencyQueryStore sub-interface gains an `IterAllDependencyRecords(ctx) (Iter[types.Dependency], error)` for completeness.

## 9. CLI migration map

Concrete call-site → new path. Builders implementing this don't need to discover them — the table is the migration plan.

| Call site | File | Today | Migrate to | Why |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `bd show --json <id>` Dependents | `cmd/bd/show_display.go:164` | `GetDependentsWithMetadata` (slice) | `IterDependentsWithMetadata` (only iterates if `--include-dependents` is set; the default shallow shape from PR #3768 stays slice) | Hub-bead OOM cliff. PR #3768 is the temporary cap; iterator is the durable fix. |
| `bd show --json <id>` Comments | `cmd/bd/show_display.go:210` | `GetIssueComments` | `IterIssueComments` | Same RAM pattern; comments can grow unboundedly on long-lived beads. |
| `bd list --json --limit 0` | `cmd/bd/list.go` (~line 728) | `SearchIssues({Limit: 0})` | `IterIssues` when Limit==0; slice path retained for `Limit > 0` | The 13 GB regression source. |
| `bd ready --json` | `cmd/bd/list.go` (~line 168 in status.go variant) | `GetReadyWork` | Slice retained (typically <100 rows; bounded structurally). No change. | Already bounded. |
| `bd events <id> --json` | wherever `GetEvents` is rendered | `GetEvents` | `IterEvents` for `--limit 0`; slice for bounded | Long event tails on hot beads. |
| `bd events --since <t> --json` | `GetAllEventsSince` caller | `GetAllEventsSince` | `IterAllEventsSince` always | Full-rig event scans are unbounded. |
| `bd wisp list --json` | `cmd/bd/wisp.go` | `ListWisps` | `IterWisps` for `--limit 0` | Wisp counts can balloon during high-traffic ticks. |
| `bd ado` (sweeps all issues) | `cmd/bd/ado.go:717,743,850` | `SearchIssues({})` | `IterIssues` always (full-table sweep) | Currently allocates an entire issues table just to walk it. |
| `bd doctor pollution` | `cmd/bd/doctor_pollution.go:25` | `SearchIssues({})` | `IterIssues` always | Same. |
| `bd find-duplicates` | `cmd/bd/find_duplicates.go:111` | `SearchIssues(filter)` | `IterIssues` if no Limit set | Same. |
| `bd lint` | `cmd/bd/lint.go:92` | `SearchIssues(filter)` | `IterIssues` if no Limit set | Same. |
| `bd label show` | `cmd/bd/label.go:188,274` | `SearchIssues({})` / `SearchIssues({ParentID})` | `IterIssues` for the unbounded `{}` case; slice for `ParentID` (typically <50 children) | The all-issues sweep is the bloat path. |
| `bd todo` | `cmd/bd/todo.go:102` | `SearchIssues(filter)` | Slice (bounded by labels filter typically) | No change. |
| `bd info --hub-counts` | `cmd/bd/info.go:65,102` | `SearchIssues(filter)` then `len()` | `CountIssues(filter)` | Cardinality only — pure count win. |
| `bd preflight` | `cmd/bd/preflight.go` (anywhere it does `len(issues)`) | `SearchIssues` + `len()` | `CountIssues` | Same. |
| Epic progress (`cmd/bd/close.go::dependents check`) | `cmd/bd/close.go:455` | `GetDependentsWithMetadata` then `len()` for "any open?" | `CountDependents(issueID)` (or `CountDependentsByStatus` if we need open vs closed split — see §11) | Hub epic close is currently O(N) on RAM. |
| `bd ping` | `cmd/bd/ping.go:54` | `SearchIssues` (just probing reachability) | `CountIssues({Limit: 1})` | Just check the connection — not the data. |
| `bd ado peer-discovery` | `cmd/bd/ado.go:850` | `SearchIssues({})` then walk | `IterIssues({})` | Full-table walk. |
| `bd completion` (id-prefix lookups) | `cmd/bd/completions.go:46` | `SearchIssues({IDPrefix})` | Slice retained (already bounded by `Limit: 50` in the filter) | No change. |

For **`gc nudge drain --inject`** (from gc-management) — the hottest callsite at every UserPromptSubmit hook — the cross-rig fix is be-aw0afh: prefer in-process gc store over `bd show --json`. The bd-side migration to `IterIssueComments`/etc. above is what makes the in-process call cheap; gc still has to do the work.

## 10. Use case — `bd list --json --limit 0` end-to-end

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["User runs bd list --json --label X --limit 0"] --> B{cmd/bd/list.go}
    B --> C{Limit == 0?}
    C -->|"yes (was 13 GB cliff)"| D[store.IterIssues ctx query filter]
    C -->|no| E[store.SearchIssues ctx query filter]
    D --> F[Backend opens cursor / sql.Rows]
    F --> G["Loop: it.Next ctx → it.Value"]
    G --> H[Encode one issue to stdout JSON]
    H --> I{more rows?}
    I -->|yes| G
    I -->|no| J[it.Close releases cursor]
    J --> K[stdout closes ]]
    E --> L[Slice in memory]
    L --> M[json.Marshal slice]
    M --> N[stdout writes whole array]
```

## 11. Action flow — IterIssues over RPC (be-oyer9z transport)

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant CLI as bd CLI
    participant Daemon as bdd daemon
    participant Backend as PG/Dolt
    CLI->>Daemon: IterStartReq query filter
    Daemon->>Backend: open cursor / sql.Rows
    Daemon-->>CLI: sessionID
    loop until done
      CLI->>Daemon: IterNextReq sessionID batchSize=100
      Daemon->>Backend: read 100 rows
      Backend-->>Daemon: 100 rows
      Daemon-->>CLI: items done=false
      CLI->>CLI: encode rows to stdout
    end
    CLI->>Daemon: IterCloseReq sessionID
    Daemon->>Backend: close cursor
    Daemon-->>CLI: ok
```

1. CLI calls `store.IterIssues(ctx, query, filter)`. The RPC client sends `Storage.IterStart` to the daemon with the query and filter.
2. Daemon receives `IterStart`, opens the SQL cursor (PG: `BEGIN; DECLARE cursor_<id> CURSOR FOR …`; Dolt: `db.QueryContext(...)` returning `sql.Rows`), allocates a session token, stashes the iterator.
3. Daemon returns the session token to the CLI.
4. CLI's `Iter.Next()` checks its prefetch buffer; if empty, sends `Storage.IterNext` with `{sessionID, batchSize: 100}`.
5. Daemon fetches up to 100 rows from the underlying iterator.
6. Daemon returns `{items: [...], done: false}` (or `done: true` if exhausted).
7. CLI buffers the batch; subsequent `Next()` calls drain it before the next RPC.
8. CLI's render loop encodes each `Value()` to stdout, never holding more than `batchSize` rows in memory.
9. When the user's loop exits (or context cancels), CLI calls `Iter.Close()`, which sends `Storage.IterClose`.
10. Daemon releases the SQL cursor and removes the session token. Idle reaper would do this anyway after 30 s as a safety net.

## 12. Data model

The architecture changes none of bd's persistent schema. The only state added is server-side iterator sessions in the daemon (in-memory only):

```mermaid
erDiagram
    DAEMON ||--o{ ITER_SESSION : "holds"
    ITER_SESSION {
        string session_id "UUID"
        time_t opened_at
        time_t last_activity_at
        string filter_json "for diagnostics only"
        sql_rows underlying "PG cursor or Dolt sql.Rows"
    }
    ITER_SESSION }|--|| BACKEND_CURSOR : "wraps"
```

There is no persistent schema migration. Everything lives in-process or on-the-wire.

## 13. Trade-offs & alternatives considered

### Why combination instead of "iterator-only"

Forcing every call site to use the iterator is purer but costs about 80 mechanical migrations across `cmd/bd/`. The slice path is fine for bounded reads (`bd show <id>`, `bd ready --limit 10`), and the conversion would be churn without RAM benefit. The combination keeps incremental migrations possible and sidesteps a giant single-PR diff.

### Why callback-style was rejected

`store.IterateIssues(ctx, filter, func(*Issue) error)` is simpler (no Close to forget) and well-known from `filepath.WalkDir`. Two reasons we don't pick it:

1. **JSON streaming is awkward.** The CLI needs to write `[`, then comma-separated objects, then `]`. A callback can only see "here's another row" — figuring out "is this the first? the last?" requires extra state. The Next()/Value() shape lets the CLI naturally handle the boundary cases.
2. **RPC fit is worse.** A callback is a coroutine; net/rpc + gob has no streams, so the daemon would have to invent server-driven "push" semantics — exactly what we're trying to avoid by picking gob in the first place. With Next()/Close(), the client polls; the server is purely request/response.

If a callback shape is wanted as a convenience (it is — for tests), provide it as a helper layered on top:

```go
func ForEachIssue(ctx context.Context, it Iter[types.Issue], fn func(*types.Issue) error) error {
    defer it.Close()
    for it.Next(ctx) {
        if err := fn(it.Value()); err != nil { return err }
    }
    return it.Err()
}
```

### Why streaming JSON writer on Storage was rejected

`WriteIssuesJSON(ctx, w io.Writer, filter)` solves the RAM problem in one method. It does so by collapsing two responsibilities (data fetch + serialization) and forecloses on:

- **Filter/transform pipelines.** `bd list --label X | jq '.[].id'` works because the CLI controls JSON formatting. If Storage emits JSON, every downstream transform (label resolution, status formatting, gc nudge consumer) fights with the writer.
- **Multiple output formats.** `bd list --format=table` and `bd list --format=jsonl` and `bd list --format=tsv` all share the same iterator path; only the renderer changes. A JSON-emitting Storage forces a rebuild for every format.
- **RPC parity.** A `WriteIssuesJSON` over net/rpc+gob is moot — the writer can't cross the wire. The daemon would still need the iterator under the hood, then immediately encode JSON server-side. We'd have two interfaces doing what one does.

Iterator + CLI-side `json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(item)` per row achieves identical RAM bounds with cleaner separation.

### Why net/rpc + gob batching instead of gRPC server-streaming

Already settled in be-ef3q3u §13: gRPC adds vendored deps (`google.golang.org/grpc` ~6 MB, `protoc` toolchain), the Storage interface is gob-friendly, and `connectrpc.com/connect` was the second-place option for similar reasons. Iterators-over-batched-net/rpc is good enough; if the daemon's hot path becomes a measured bottleneck, the migration to connect-go is mechanical at that point.

### Why `IterReadyWork` — isn't it already bounded?

Today, yes. `bd ready` typically returns <100 rows. But the same method backs `gc sling`'s queue inspection and the deacon patrols, both of which operate over thousands of beads in worst case. Cheaper to add `IterReadyWork` now than retrofit later.

### Why aggregate methods are P0 even though they're "just" `len()` replacements

They're P0 *because* they're trivial. Each `SearchIssues + len()` site materializes the entire result for one int64. The cumulative RAM saving is large; the per-site change is one line. High leverage.

### Per-row hydration cost

Iterator path makes per-row label hydration the dominant cost (one extra round-trip per row). The slice path can amortize hydration via a single batched query (`SELECT issue_id, label FROM labels WHERE issue_id IN (...)`). For unbounded queries this is fine — we're saving GBs at the cost of microseconds per row. For bounded queries the slice path's amortization is preserved (we don't migrate them).

If iterator-side hydration becomes a measured bottleneck, the implementation can buffer N rows internally, batch-hydrate, then expose them through Next() — no contract change.

### Why we don't introduce `context.Context` in `Value()` / `Err()` / `Close()`

`Next(ctx)` carries the cancellation signal. `Close()` should be reliable even when `ctx` is canceled (otherwise we leak DB cursors on context expiry — exactly the bug we're avoiding). Mirrors `database/sql.Rows`.

## 14. Security controls

| Control | Mechanism | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Iterator session auth | Inherits daemon's Unix-socket file ACL (mode 0600) | No new auth surface; only owner can connect to the socket. |
| Session-token guessing | UUIDv4 sessionIDs (16 random bytes) | Even if an attacker had socket access, predicting a session token to drain another iterator is impractical. |
| Iterator session leakage | Idle reaper (30 s default) + cap at 64 sessions | DoS via "open many iterators" is bounded. `ErrTooManyIterators` returned to clients past the cap. |
| Cursor injection | Filter values still parameterized via existing PG `add()` placeholder helper / Dolt `?` placeholders | Same SQL-injection posture as slice path; iterator does not change query construction. |
| Sentinel error round-trip | gob-encoded `{kind, msg}` envelope from be-oyer9z | `errors.Is(it.Err(), storage.ErrNotFound)` behaves identically across transports (parity-tested). |

## 15. Integrations

| Direction | Other side | Protocol | Auth | SLA notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **CLI → Storage (in-process)** | Local DB cursor (PG / Dolt) | direct Go call | filesystem (storage handle holder) | hot-path single-row read MUST not regress >5% on bounded queries (NFR-02). |
| **CLI → bdd daemon (Option A from be-ef3q3u)** | Unix socket | net/rpc + gob | filesystem ACL | iter batch round-trip target <2 ms per `IterNext` for 100 rows on localhost. |
| **bdd daemon → Storage** | DB cursor | direct Go call | same handle daemon already holds | cursors held in-process; daemon serializes via existing concurrency-safe Storage methods. |
| **gc nudge drain → bd CLI** | subprocess (current) | exec | inherited | parallel work in be-aw0afh — moves to in-process call once gc-side store is wired. Iterator on the bd side makes this in-process call cheap. |
| **External Go API (`beads.go`)** | direct import | Go API | n/a | New iterator methods are additive on `storage.Storage`. Existing public types/aliases unchanged. No external API break. |

## 16. Risks

| Risk | Likelihood | Impact | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Per-row hydration tanks throughput on Iter paths | medium | medium | Buffered batch-hydrate inside iterator (transparent to caller); benchmark gates merge. |
| Cursor leak on RPC client crash | medium | medium | Server-side idle reaper (30 s default); session cap; daemon restart wipes all sessions cleanly. |
| Two interfaces to maintain (slice + iter) drift over time | medium | low | Parity tests in `internal/storage/parity/` exercise both shapes against the same fixtures; CI is the safety net. |
| gob encoding of `Iter[T]` types accidentally tries to encode interface fields with non-public concrete types | low | high | Iterator wire types are concrete (`IterNextResp{Items []*types.Issue}`); the iterator interface itself never crosses the wire — only batches do. |
| Migrating callers introduces subtle behavior changes (e.g., goroutine ordering) | low | medium | Keep slice methods unchanged; migrate one caller at a time; parity tests on the migrated callers' user-visible output. |
| Iterator-with-hydration deadlocks on PG when the same connection is borrowed for label hydration | medium | medium | Iterator must use a **dedicated connection** held for its lifetime; hydration runs on the same connection sequentially. PG impl uses `pgxpool.AcquireFunc` style. |
| Daemon iterator state grows unbounded under buggy clients | low | medium | Hard cap (64 default) + idle reaper + emit `iter_sessions_active` stat for observability. |
| Existing callers depending on `len()` of slice as a side effect (e.g., `if len(issues) == 0`) | low | low | `Count*` methods cover this exactly; migration is mechanical. |

## 17. Guardrails (downstream agents)

These constraints carry forward to designer / builder / reviewer:

- **Slice methods MUST NOT be deprecated.** Bounded callers stay on the slice path; mass migration is anti-goal.
- **Iterators MUST always have a deferred Close().** Linter warning in CI for `Iter*(...)` calls without subsequent `defer .Close()` is a P1 follow-up. Cursor leaks are the primary risk.
- **No new vendored deps.** Iterator implementation stays within stdlib + already-vendored modules. (Constraint inherited from be-ef3q3u §4.)
- **Iterator return shape is unified — `Iter[T]`.** Do NOT introduce per-type iterator types (`IssueIter`, `EventIter`). The generic shape is the contract.
- **Per-row hydration must use a dedicated connection.** PG iterator must hold its own pool connection for the iterator's lifetime; sharing across iterators causes deadlock.
- **Migration is incremental, one CLI command per PR.** Do NOT attempt a single PR that migrates all 80+ call sites. Each migration includes a parity-test entry.
- **Iterator over RPC SHALL NOT be implemented before be-oyer9z lands.** The daemon framework is the prerequisite; ship in-process iterators first, layer RPC iterators on top once the daemon exists.
- **Default RPC batch size is 100, configurable via `daemon_iter_batch`.** Do not hardcode in client code.

## 18. Decomposition (handoff)

The architecture decomposes into the following child beads, each routed to designer for layout and acceptance criteria. Listed in suggested ship order.

1. **Add `Iter[T]` interface + `Iter*` methods on Storage (shape only)** — Storage interface change + skeleton implementations in PG and Dolt. No CLI migrations yet. Parity tests added. This unblocks everything else.
2. **Add `Count*` methods on Storage + parity tests** — independent of #1; can ship in parallel. Smaller, easier first PR.
3. **Migrate `bd show --json` Dependents/Comments to iterators** — durable replacement for PR #3768's stripped-fields hot fix. Highest-RAM payoff.
4. **Migrate `bd list --json --limit 0` to iterator** — kills the 13 GB regression source.
5. **Migrate hot bulk callers (`bd ado`, `bd doctor pollution`, `bd find-duplicates`, `bd lint`, `bd label show`, `bd ado peer-discovery`)** — full-table sweeps that currently materialize.
6. **Migrate count-only callers (`bd info --hub-counts`, `bd preflight`, `bd close` epic-closure check, `bd ping`)** — pure-count wins; one-line edits.
7. **Migrate event/wisp callers (`bd events`, `bd wisp list`)** — same pattern as #3, lower urgency.
8. **Daemon RPC iterator integration (depends on be-oyer9z landing first)** — cursor-token protocol, idle reaper, session cap, parity tests across transports.

Builder note: the `internal/storage/parity/` harness is the reference for what "implemented correctly" means. Each child bead's done-when criteria includes "parity tests pass on both PG and Dolt".

## 19. Out of scope

- **PG SearchIssues filter coverage gap (be-jdeief).** Parallel work; iterator inherits whatever filters exist at any commit.
- **Hot fix follow-ups for PR #3768.** Tracked in be-4d36f2.
- **Cross-rig fix for `gc nudge drain` subprocess storm.** Tracked in be-aw0afh; bd-side iterator makes the in-process call cheap, gc-side does the actual switch.
- **Refactoring duplicate filter logic between PG and Dolt.** Existing canonical builder (`issueops/filters.go`) already does most of it; out of scope for this architecture.
- **`bd export`/`bd import` JSONL streaming.** Already streams via `json.Encoder` per line — no slurping issue. Out of scope.
close_reason: Architecture posted to bead body. 8 child design beads created: be-jaavsb (Iter interface), be-rqyhbb (Count methods), be-775o60 (bd show migration), be-c40q2v (bd list migration), be-7hvi6c (bulk sweeps), be-pkg36q (count migrations), be-f68axd (events/wisps), be-60kmhm (daemon RPC iterator). Blocks/discovered-from dependencies wired.

title: Cross-rig: gc event emit per-mutation subprocess storm — investigate from gc-management
description:
## Rig investigator handoff

**Original bead**: be-dkyz2d ([investigator] gc event emit per-mutation subprocess storm — 5+ procs per bead lifecycle).

The bead's deliverables span both rigs but lean toward gc-management:

1. \"Confirm: is `gc event emit` always a fork-exec, or sometimes in-process?\" → **gc-management** code (cmd/gc, internal/event)
2. \"Could events be batched and emitted in-process via a single fork per bead operation (or per tick)?\" → **gc-management** event-emission API
3. \"What share of total bd subprocess invocations comes from event emission vs. from agent reads (bd list, bd show, bd ready)?\" → **cross-rig** profiling (process-tree sampling across both rigs)
4. \"If subprocess-per-event is unavoidable, can the bd binary's cold-start path be slimmed (skip auto-import entirely when only emitting events, avoid loading config schemas)?\" → **beads** code (cmd/bd PreRun + auto-import)

Three of four deliverables require gc-management visibility. The rig-scoped beads investigator can only reason about #4 from a partial view. Escalating to the city-level deep-investigator who can reach across both rigs.

## Evidence so far (from be-dkyz2d notes)

Mayor 2026-05-06: a single bead lifecycle (gm-sdr75s, order:dolt-health) spawned at least 5 short-lived `gc event emit ...` subprocesses, one per audit event (bead.created, bead.updated×3, bead.closed). Each ~50 MB RSS, ~2.6 GB VSS, 105-107% CPU, lifetime a few seconds. At soak (N agents × M writes/tick), spawn rate compounds.

Even with the be-4d36f2 bd show --json hot fix landed in PR #3768, the subprocess-spawn RATE itself remains. The bd-side cold-start cost (auto-import + config load) is paid for every spawn.

## Cross-rig leads

- **gc-management cmd/gc**: where does `gc event emit` actually emit from? Find the call site for bead.created, bead.updated, bead.closed events.
- **gc-management internal/event** (or similar): emission API. In-process vs subprocess decision.
- **gc-management hooks**: settings.json hooks (specifically `gc nudge drain --inject` referenced in be-4d36f2 notes) that drive bd subprocess invocation rate.
- **beads cmd/bd PreRun**: what loads on every bd binary startup. auto-import path. Could a `--just-emit-event` fast path skip most of it.

## Trail leaves the rig

`gc event emit` source lives in `/home/jaword/projects/gc-management/...`, not in `/home/jaword/projects/beads/...`. The rig-scoped beads investigator cannot read it. Escalating.

## Refs

- be-4d36f2 — bd RAM bloat (related; hot fix in PR #3768)
- be-b0t — bd transient subprocess auto-import cost (mentioned in be-dkyz2d but the bead may not exist anymore — verify before relying)

title: [postgres] needs-tests: integration coverage for CreateIssue + custom issue_type/status (be-rhtega)
description:
Follow-up to be-rhtega. The fix landed without integration test coverage for CreateIssue with a custom issue_type (e.g. session). Author verified live but the behavior is not pinned in CI.

title: [investigator] gc event emit per-mutation subprocess storm — 5+ procs per bead lifecycle
notes:
## Observed (mayor session 2026-05-06)

A single bead lifecycle (gm-sdr75s, order:dolt-health) spawned at least
5 separate `gc event emit ...` subprocesses, one each for:

- bead.created
- bead.updated (3×, for label additions)
- bead.closed

Each subprocess: ~50 MB RSS, ~2.6 GB VSS, 105-107% CPU. Lifetime is
short (a few seconds) but at scale (city tick rate × bead-mutating
agents), this accumulates significantly.

For a soak load with N agents each doing M bead writes per tick,
this is N*M subprocess spawns per tick. Each one pays the bd-binary
cold-start cost (small but real) plus the auto-import path (large
when JSONL is present and fresh).

## Why this matters

The user observation — "users should not need 120+ gigs of ram to just
avoid OOM" — is sharpened by this pattern. Even with the be-4d36f2 bd
show --json fix landed (PR #3768), every bead mutation forks ~5
short-lived bd subprocesses. Each one's RSS is bounded but the spawn
RATE matters for kernel memory pressure and page-cache churn.

## Investigator deliverables

1. Confirm: is `gc event emit` always a fork-exec, or sometimes
   in-process?
2. Could events be batched and emitted in-process via a single fork
   per bead operation (or per tick)?
3. What share of total bd subprocess invocations comes from event
   emission vs. from agent reads (bd list, bd show, bd ready)?
4. If subprocess-per-event is unavoidable, can the bd binary's
   cold-start path be slimmed (skip auto-import entirely when only
   emitting events, avoid loading config schemas)?

## Refs

- be-4d36f2 — the headline bd RAM bug; PR #3768 lands the hot fix
- be-b0t (lost in earlier dolt confusion, would need re-filing) —
  bd transient subprocess auto-import cost


## 2026-05-07 15:40 UTC — escalated to deep-investigator

Three of four deliverables (Q1-Q3) require gc-management code visibility, which the rig-scoped beads investigator doesn't have. Q4 (slim bd cold-start) is beads-side but only relevant if Q1-Q2 conclude that fork-exec is unavoidable.

Escalated to deep-investigator via **be-aw0afh** with the cross-rig leads I could trace from the beads side.

title: [follow-up be-035] bd update --status=closed bypasses assignee authority guard
description:
## Context

be-07y reviewed and passed the be-035 fix (commit 7a925e304) which added
`validation.AssigneeMatches` to `bd close`. During review, a parallel
silent-data-loss surface was identified that the fix does not cover:

`bd update <id> --status=closed` writes the closure through
`issueStore.UpdateIssue` (cmd/bd/update.go:366) without going through
`validateIssueClosable` or the new `AssigneeMatches` validator.

## Reproducer (analogous to be-035)

1. Session A claims bead X via `bd update X --claim` → assignee = A.
2. Session B re-claims X → assignee = B.
3. Session A calls `bd update X --status=closed` (instead of `bd close`).
4. UpdateIssue persists the status change. No authority check.
5. Bead is closed by the wrong actor — same silent-data-loss class as
   be-035, just via a different command surface.

## Required behavior

- `bd update` MUST run the same authority guard when `--status=closed`
  is being applied. (Or, equivalently, route close-via-update through
  the same validator chain as `bd close`.)
- The error message and exit code should match `bd close` (non-zero,
  "assignee is X, actor is Y; reclaim or use --force to override").

## Fix sketch

In `cmd/bd/update.go` around line 63 (where `updates["status"] = status`
is set), if the new status is `"closed"`, run the same chain that
`validateIssueClosable` runs against the current issue (fetch the issue
first, then `validation.Chain(NotTemplate, NotPinned(force), AssigneeMatches(actor, force))`).
Bail with non-zero exit on guard failure, matching the `bd close`
ergonomics.

## Acceptance

1. New integration test in `cmd/bd/update_embedded_test.go` (or
   sibling) reproduces actor != assignee via `bd update --status=closed`,
   asserts non-zero exit, stderr names actor and assignee, bead status
   stays at its prior value in the store.
2. Same reproducer works with `--force` to override (parity with
   `bd close --force`).

## Severity

P2 not P1 because:
- be-035 covered the primary `bd close` surface used by 99% of agents.
- This is a less-traveled path; agents rarely close via `bd update`.
- But it's the same silent-data-loss class; should be closed for
  defense in depth.

## Discovered from

be-07y review of commit 7a925e304.
close_reason: validateIssueClosable now requires actor param + AssigneeMatches; bd update --status=closed runs full guard; --force flag added for override parity. Commit e8647db52.

notes:
## Spike Results

### Test written
`internal/storage/dolt/joiniter_spike_test.go::TestJoinIterPanic_Spike`

Covers 5 JOIN/EXISTS shapes on go-mysql-server v0.20.1-0.20260507202550-43d6daf5958b:

| shape | description | workaround location |
|---|---|---|
| inner_join_issues_deps | `JOIN issues+dependencies` | GetMoleculeProgress |
| correlated_exists_subquery | `EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM deps WHERE dep.issue_id = outer.id)` | ComputeBlockedIDsInTx |
| double_correlated_exists | nested EXISTS for blocked+active check | ComputeBlockedIDsInTx |
| non_correlated_in_subquery | `WHERE id IN (SELECT issue_id FROM deps)` — baseline | n/a (safe, in prod) |
| multi_column_filter_with_type_subquery | type+status+priority combined | ready_work.go |

### Methodology
Each sub-test wraps the query in a `recover()` closure. If the panic fires: `t.Error` (bug still present). If no panic: `t.Skip` with a note that the workaround is liftable.

### Test cannot run without Dolt server
The test uses `setupTestStore` which requires either Docker (`dolthub/dolt-sql-server:1.88.1`) or an embedded Dolt engine (CGO build). CI must run with Dolt available to produce results.

### Known safe shape (already in production)
Non-correlated `IN (SELECT ...)` subqueries do not panic. This is the pattern used throughout ready_work.go, filters.go, and the Q1/Q3 additions in this branch.

### Recommended CI step
Run: `go test -tags gms_pure_go -v -run TestJoinIterPanic_Spike ./internal/storage/dolt/`
with a live Dolt server. Report skip vs error for each sub-test to determine which workarounds can be lifted.

title: bd perf Q4: make bd stats blocked-count optional
description:
# CLI UX Design — `bd stats --no-blocked` (bd-f5zqs)

**Bead:** bd-f5zqs
**Designer:** beads/designer
**Date:** 2026-05-17
**Architect spec:** bd-f5zqs (bd perf Q4)
**Status:** Design → builder handoff

---

## 1. Summary

`bd stats` (alias: `bd status`) gains a `--no-blocked` flag that skips the
`computeBlockedIDs` traversal. The blocked count line is replaced with a
muted "(skipped)" placeholder so the output table stays structurally intact.
JSON output changes `blocked_issues` from `int` to `*int` (nullable) and
adds a `blocked_count_skipped` boolean for machine-readable detection.

---

## 2. Flag

```
--no-blocked   Skip blocked-count computation (much faster on large rigs).
               Blocked count is shown as "(skipped)" in human output and
               null in JSON output.
```

**No short alias.** This is a performance escape hatch, not a daily flag.
Short aliases invite accidental use.

**Position in `--help`:** After `--no-activity`, before `--json`:

```
      --assigned      Show issues assigned to current user only
      --no-activity   Skip git activity summary (faster)
      --no-blocked    Skip blocked-count computation (faster on large rigs)
      --json          Output in JSON format
```

This groups `--no-*` performance flags together, which aids discoverability.

---

## 3. Long help addition

Append to `statusCmd.Long`, after the `bd status --no-activity` example line:

```
  bd status --no-blocked             # Skip slow blocked-count scan (faster)
  bd stats --no-blocked --json       # JSON output without blocked count
```

Add to the `Use cases:` section:

```
  - Fast CI status checks that don't need blocked-count accuracy
```

---

## 4. Human-readable output

### 4a. Normal (with `--no-blocked`)

```
📊 Issue Database Status

Summary:
  Total Issues:           2741
  Open:                    305
  In Progress:               3
  Blocked:         (skipped)
  Closed:                 2280
  Ready to Work:           263
```

The `(skipped)` value uses `ui.MutedStyle`. The `Blocked:` label stays
in the same column, plain text, so the table remains scannable with the
same column width. Right-align `(skipped)` to column 32 (same as the
numeric values).

**Do not** omit the line. An absent row causes confusion about whether
blocked counting is broken or intentionally skipped. The placeholder
signals intent.

### 4b. Zero-blocked edge case

When `computeBlockedIDs` would return 0, the line currently shows `0`
(no red color — `ui.RenderFail` on "0" still renders in red, which is
misleading). This is an existing bug outside bd-f5zqs scope; flag in
close notes for a follow-up bead.

---

## 5. JSON output changes

### 5a. `Statistics` struct change

Change `BlockedIssues int` → `BlockedIssues *int` in `types.Statistics`:

```go
type Statistics struct {
    TotalIssues             int     `json:"total_issues"`
    OpenIssues              int     `json:"open_issues"`
    InProgressIssues        int     `json:"in_progress_issues"`
    ClosedIssues            int     `json:"closed_issues"`
    BlockedIssues           *int    `json:"blocked_issues"`   // nullable
    DeferredIssues          int     `json:"deferred_issues"`
    ReadyIssues             int     `json:"ready_issues"`
    PinnedIssues            int     `json:"pinned_issues"`
    EpicsEligibleForClosure int     `json:"epics_eligible_for_closure"`
    AverageLeadTime         float64 `json:"average_lead_time_hours"`
}
```

**Migration note:** All callers that dereference `BlockedIssues` without
nil-check will need updating. Builder must grep for `stats.BlockedIssues`
and `s.BlockedIssues` across `cmd/bd/` and `internal/`. The human-output
path at `status.go:108` must nil-check before formatting.

### 5b. StatusOutput wrapper change

Add `BlockedCountSkipped` to the `StatusOutput` struct (or directly in the
JSON output):

```go
type StatusOutput struct {
    Summary            *types.Statistics      `json:"summary"`
    BlockedCountSkipped bool                  `json:"blocked_count_skipped,omitempty"`
    RecentActivity     *RecentActivitySummary `json:"recent_activity,omitempty"`
}
```

`blocked_count_skipped` is `omitempty` — it appears only when `true`.
This avoids polluting the default JSON output with a new field.

### 5c. JSON shape comparison

**Default (no flag):**
```json
{
  "summary": {
    "blocked_issues": 42,
    ...
  }
}
```

**With `--no-blocked`:**
```json
{
  "summary": {
    "blocked_issues": null,
    ...
  },
  "blocked_count_skipped": true
}
```

Callers can check `blocked_count_skipped` to distinguish `null` (skipped)
from a future case where `blocked_issues` might be 0.

---

## 6. Style assignments

| Element                    | Style           | Rationale                          |
|----------------------------|-----------------|------------------------------------|
| `(skipped)` value          | `ui.MutedStyle` | Informational, not a problem       |
| `Blocked:` label           | plain text      | Same as other stat labels          |

No new colors. Existing palette only.

---

## 7. Accessibility audit

| Concern                     | Status | Notes                                              |
|-----------------------------|--------|----------------------------------------------------|
| Screen reader compatibility | ✓ Pass | Plain text "(skipped)" is fully readable           |
| Color contrast              | ✓ Pass | MutedStyle gray passes WCAG AA on dark and light   |
| No-color mode (`NO_COLOR=1`)| ✓ Pass | "(skipped)" text carries meaning; color is enhancement only |
| Non-TTY piped output        | ✓ Pass | ShouldUseColor() returns false; no ANSI leaks      |
| Information without color   | ✓ Pass | The "(skipped)" placeholder preserves information  |
| Flag discoverability        | ✓ Pass | Grouped with --no-activity in --help               |

WCAG 2.1 AA: **No new violations.**

---

## 8. Caller audit (builder must check)

Before submitting the PR, grep for all callers of `statistics.BlockedIssues`
or `stats.BlockedIssues` and add nil guards:

```bash
grep -rn "BlockedIssues" cmd/bd/ internal/
```

Expected callers:
- `cmd/bd/status.go:108` — human output render
- `cmd/bd/status.go:getAssignedStatistics` — constructs Statistics directly;
  must set `BlockedIssues` as `*int` pointer
- Any integration tests that assert `BlockedIssues` value

---

## 9. Backward compatibility

- `blocked_issues: null` is valid JSON; existing parsers that do
  `obj.blocked_issues || 0` will degrade gracefully to 0.
- `blocked_count_skipped` is `omitempty`, so default output is unchanged.
- Human output table structure is unchanged (same columns, same width).
- `bd stats` (default, no flag) behavior is identical to current.

NFR-06 is satisfied.

---

## 10. Follow-up (out of scope for bd-f5zqs)

The existing `ui.RenderFail("0")` on the Blocked line renders 0 in red,
which implies "problem" when there are no blocked issues. This is a separate
cosmetic bug: `Blocked: 0` should render plain or green. File as a child bead
from the builder session when submitting bd-f5zqs.
notes:
Derived from bd-3e4at architecture analysis (Q4).

## Goal
`bd stats` is dominated by `computeBlockedIDs`, which scans issues + wisps + dependencies + wisp_dependencies on every fresh invocation. Make blocked-count opt-in (or async) so the cheap aggregate path returns instantly.

## What changes
- Add `--no-blocked` flag to `bd stats` (and corresponding storage path that doesn't call `computeBlockedIDs`).
- When omitted, the CLI returns the cheap `ScanIssueCountsInTx` aggregate immediately and renders blocked count as `(skipped)` or omits the line.
- Default behavior stays the same (computes blocked) for backward compat.

## Optional follow-up Q4b
If the spike (separate bead) confirms Dolt joinIter is no longer panicking on cross-table CTEs, switch `computeBlockedIDs` to `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM ready_issues` and similar CTE-based queries. Cleaner, no Go-side traversal, indexes do the work.

## What stays the same
- `GetStatistics` interface preserved (blocked count still populated when requested).
- `ScanIssueCountsInTx` aggregate remains the cheap-path baseline.

## Why
On a 49k-bead rig with active blocking dependencies, `bd stats` takes ~2s. The aggregate alone takes <50ms. The other 1.95s is the Go-side blocked-set traversal. Many `bd stats` callers (CI dashboards, periodic reports) don't need the blocked figure on every invocation.

## Acceptance

title: bd perf Q3: shift SearchIssues to id-shrunk Pattern B for Limit > 0
description:
# Design Review: bd perf Q3 — SearchIssues id-shrunk Pattern B (bd-co6m6)

**Bead:** bd-co6m6
**Designer:** beads/designer
**Date:** 2026-05-17
**Status:** No UX changes — approved, route to builder

---

## Verdict: No UX Design Scope

`searchTableInTx` is an internal storage function. Switching from a 47-col
projection to a SELECT id + hydration step is purely a query optimization.
Result-set ordering and content are preserved per the architect's spec:
> "Result-set ordering matches Pattern A byte-for-byte across representative filter shapes."

**User-visible behavior:** Unchanged. Faster `bd list` and `bd query` output,
same results.

**Accessibility:** N/A — no output changes.

---

## Routing

Ready for builder. No design iteration needed.
notes:
Derived from bd-3e4at architecture analysis (Q3).

## Goal
For `searchTableInTx` calls with `Limit > 0`, change the SQL projection from `SELECT <47 cols>` to `SELECT id`, then call `GetIssuesByIDsInTx` to hydrate only the result rows. Mirror the pattern already used in `scanIssueIDs` and `GetStaleIssuesInTx`.

## What changes
- Modify `searchTableInTx` (or add a parallel helper) to:
  1. Run `SELECT id FROM <table> WHERE <where> ORDER BY priority ASC, created_at DESC, id ASC LIMIT <n>`.
  2. Call `GetIssuesByIDsInTx` for the ID set.
  3. Reorder by the id slice to preserve the ORDER BY (already-implemented pattern in `scanIssueIDs`).
- Keep the current 47-col projection path for `Limit == 0` (unlimited) since Pattern B has no benefit there.
- Add a filter flag `NoIDShrink` for any caller that needs the existing single-pass behavior (not expected, but kept as escape valve).

## What stays the same
- `IssueSelectColumns` and `ScanIssueFrom` unchanged.
- Label hydration still happens via `GetLabelsForIssuesInTx` on the result IDs.
- Wisps merge logic unchanged (composes with Q2 above).

## Why
The default `bd list` limit is 50; agent mode 20; query default 50. Today every call streams every candidate row's 47 columns into Go. Pattern B converts that into a 1-col candidate scan + a 50-row hydration. On a 49k corpus this turns a ~250ms query into ~30ms.

## Acceptance
- Result-set ordering matches Pattern A byte-for-byte across representative filter shapes.
- Bench delta on 10k corpus: bd list with default limit shows ≥5x speedup.
- No regression on `bd list --all` (Limit=0) — Pattern A still used.

## Pointers
- Reference impl: `internal/storage/dolt/dependencies.go:scanIssueIDs`.
- Stale uses the same trick: `internal/storage/issueops/stale.go:GetStaleIssuesInTx`.
- Caller to update: `internal/storage/issueops/search.go:searchTableInTx`.

title: bd perf Q2+Q5: skip wisps merge when not needed in SearchIssues
description:
# Design Review: bd perf Q2+Q5 — Skip Wisps Merge (bd-qi4qr)

**Bead:** bd-qi4qr
**Designer:** beads/designer
**Date:** 2026-05-17
**Status:** No UX changes — approved, route to builder

---

## Verdict: No UX Design Scope

`IssueFilter.SkipWisps bool` is an internal filter flag. No new user-visible
CLI flags are introduced. The optimization is transparent to the user: commands
return the same results, just faster.

**User-visible behavior preserved:**
- `bd list --include-infra` still merges wisps (existing behavior)
- Mail commands still see wisps merged
- The per-process wisps row-count cache (Q5) is invisible to users

**Accessibility:** N/A — no output changes.

---

## Risk note for builder

The SkipWisps default is conservatively opt-in per the architect's spec. Verify
that every call site that flips `SkipWisps=true` is covered by a regression
test asserting wisps DO NOT appear. The risk of a missing test is silent
disappearance of ephemeral results, which is hard to notice in CI.

---

## Routing

Ready for builder. No design iteration needed.
notes:
Derived from bd-3e4at architecture analysis (Q2 + Q5).

## Goal
Eliminate the unconditional full-table wisps scan that `SearchIssues` performs on every read when `filter.Ephemeral == nil`.

## What changes
- Add `IssueFilter.SkipWisps bool` flag (Q2).
- Default callers to `SkipWisps=true` where appropriate: `cmd/bd/count.go`, `cmd/bd/query.go`, and the default path of `cmd/bd/list.go` (NOT `--include-infra`).
- Preserve current behavior for callers that legitimately need wisps merged (mail, agent-state, list with `--include-infra`).
- Add a per-process wisps row-count cache on `DoltStore` (Q5). When count is 0, short-circuit the wisps merge regardless of `SkipWisps`.
- Cache invalidation: clear on writes that touch wisps (CreateWisp, etc.). Cache TTL is bounded by CLI process lifetime, so the staleness window is small.

## What stays the same
- `searchTableInTx` continues to support both modes (issues-only and issues+wisps merge).
- Wisps schema and routing logic unchanged.

## Why
On rigs with 16K+ wisps, every `bd query` / `bd list` / `bd count` pays a full wisps scan that almost never produces useful results. On rigs with 0 wisps (most rigs), the merge is always wasted.

## Acceptance
- `bd query 'status=open'` time on a rig with 16K+ wisps drops by ≥80%.
- On rigs with 0 wisps, the wisps query never runs after the first cache fill.
- Mail commands and `bd list --include-infra` still see wisps merged (regression test).

## Pointers
- Search merge logic: `internal/storage/issueops/search.go:SearchIssuesInTx`.
- Wisps schema: `internal/storage/schema/migrations/0020_create_wisps.up.sql`.
- DoltStore cache pattern (use `computeBlockedIDs` cache as model): `internal/storage/dolt/queries.go:computeBlockedIDs`.

## Risks
- `SkipWisps=true` on the wrong caller hides ephemeral results. Default conservatively; explicit opt-in per call site; add tests for the few callers that flip it.

# Design Review: bd perf Q1 — `bd count` SQL aggregate (bd-xoi0x)

**Bead:** bd-xoi0x
**Designer:** beads/designer
**Date:** 2026-05-17
**Status:** No UX changes — approved, route to builder

---

## Verdict: No UX Design Scope

`bd count` output format is unchanged. The switch from materialize+len to
SQL `COUNT(*)` is purely an internal query optimization.

**Human output:** Single integer, same as today. No new flags, no format changes.

**JSON output:** Existing shape preserved per the architect's spec:
> "Output format for bd count (single integer; grouped map for --by-* flags)" — unchanged.

**Accessibility:** N/A — no output changes.

---

## One implementation note for builder

`bd count --by-label` uses a JOIN on `labels` (and `wisp_labels`). Verify
that the JOIN does not double-count issues tagged with multiple matching
labels when a filter matches multiple labels. The property test
`len(SearchIssues(filter)) == CountIssues(filter)` in the acceptance criteria
covers this, but explicitly include a multi-label case in the test corpus.

---

## Routing

Ready for builder. No design iteration needed.
notes:
Derived from bd-3e4at architecture analysis (Q1).

## Goal
Replace `bd count`'s materialize-then-len pattern with a SQL `COUNT(*)` aggregate.

## What changes
- New storage method: `Storage.CountIssues(ctx, filter) (int, error)`.
- New storage method: `Storage.CountIssuesByGroup(ctx, filter, groupBy) (map[string]int, error)`.
- Reuses `BuildIssueFilterClauses` for the WHERE.
- Wisps count is added only when `filter.Ephemeral == nil` (preserves current semantics).
- Group-by-label uses a JOIN on `labels` (and `wisp_labels`); other groupings emit `GROUP BY <col>`.

## What stays the same
- `IssueFilter` shape and validation.
- Wisps merge semantics (still merges by default).
- Output format for `bd count` (single integer; grouped map for `--by-*` flags).

## Why
On a 49k-bead rig, `bd count` takes 21.6s — almost all of that is row materialization in Go after fetching every column from issues + wisps. SQL `COUNT(*)` returns in milliseconds.

## Acceptance
- `len(SearchIssues(filter)) == CountIssues(filter)` for representative filter shapes (property test).
- Bench delta on 10k corpus: count shows ≥10x speedup vs SearchIssues+len baseline.
- `bd count --by-status`, `--by-priority`, `--by-type`, `--by-assignee`, `--by-label` all return identical results to current behavior.
- Implements on both `dolt` and `embeddeddolt` storage backends.

## Pointers
- Filter clause builder: `internal/storage/issueops/filters.go:BuildIssueFilterClauses`.
- Existing aggregate as model: `internal/storage/issueops/statistics.go:ScanIssueCountsInTx`.
- CLI to update: `cmd/bd/count.go`.

1. **Wrapper extension shape.** runBench takes a benchHooks struct
   with three nil-by-default func fields (AfterSetup,

**Reviewer:** beads/reviewer

### Findings

No blockers. Findings list is empty for severity ≥ low.

### Validation performed

| Check | Tags | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `go build` | `gms_pure_go` | clean |
| `go vet` | `gms_pure_go integration_pg integration_parity` | clean |

| Existing PG integration tests (TestSmokePath, TestRoundtripIdempotency, TestConcurrentReads, TestAddCommentWritesEvent, TestConnectionUsesUTC) | `gms_pure_go integration_pg` | PASS (3.3s) — confirms testfixture T→TB widening is backwards-compatible |

Sample bench delta (run-to-run jitter on 32-thread box, not for regression
baseline):
```
BenchmarkBdReady-32   ~5.5ms median   257 KiB/op   1708 allocs/op
BenchmarkBdList-32    ~4.3ms median   340 KiB/op   2256 allocs/op
BenchmarkBdCreate-32  ~452µs median   6.9 KiB/op    132 allocs/op
```

### Acceptance criteria

- [x] AC#1 — `make bench-postgres` runs cleanly locally and emits a
  benchstat-compatible artifact. **Verified.**
- [—] AC#2 — `make bench-postgres` wired into `test-postgres` CI job
  (be-6fk.6.followup) as informational step. **Properly deferred to
  be-ekw** (status=open, OPEN, gated on mayor greenlight per the
  local-only constraint). The deferral is contextually correct and the
  follow-up bead exists with adequate scope.
- [x] AC#3 — Benchmark wrapper exposes at least one extension point.
  `benchHooks{AfterSetup, BeforeTimedLoop, AfterTimedLoop}` with three
  nil-by-default func fields, dispatched in well-defined order around
  `b.ResetTimer`/`b.StopTimer`. The follow-up memory + reliability bead
  can populate any subset without rewriting the bench bodies.

### Reviewer focus areas (per builder handoff)

1. **Wrapper extension shape.** Plain `benchHooks` struct of `func`
   fields is the right surface for v1. An interface or
   options-with-callback contract would be heavier than today's needs
   warrant; the follow-up can introduce richer typing if the memory
   probe demands it. **OK as designed.**
2. **Seed shape.** 50 parents + 50 children, half blocked, shared
   across all three benchmarks. Comparability across BdReady/BdList is
   the right trade. BdCreate paying the realistic per-row index cost
   on a seeded store is more useful than a cold-insert micro-benchmark
   that wouldn't reflect production hot-path behavior. **OK as
   designed.**
3. **`-count=6` default.** Correct floor for benchstat's ≥6 samples at
   confidence 0.95. Bumping to 10 buys ~25% tighter intervals for
   ~67% more wall time; not worth it for a local-loop tool whose
   purpose is informational delta. **OK as designed.**

### Security walk (OWASP Top 10)

- **Injection:** testfixture's `createDatabase`/`dropDatabaseForce`
  continue to gate `dbName` through the `safeDBName` regex before
  fmt-interpolating into DDL. `randomSuffix(testing.TB)` produces
  hex-only output. No new injection surface introduced by this diff.
  (`internal/storage/postgres/testfixture/testfixture.go:158-171`)
- **Command injection in shell:** `scripts/benchstat-postgres.sh`
  uses `set -euo pipefail`, `mapfile -t`, and quoted expansions. The
  candidate-path loop quotes both the iterator var and array
  elements. Filenames are constrained to `bench/postgres-<short-sha>.txt`
  where SHA is hex. No injection vector.
- **Secrets:** No secrets introduced; testfixture's testcontainers
  uses literal `bd`/`bd` for ephemeral container creds (existing
  behavior, unchanged).
- **Build-tag isolation:** `//go:build integration_pg` correctly
  gates benchmark_test.go behind the same tag as the existing PG
  integration suite, so the benchmarks ship dark in default builds.
- **Dependencies:** No new third-party deps. testcontainers,
  pgx, and the perf/benchstat install path were already in the
  module graph.

### Style notes (non-blocking)

- `defer store.Close()` discards the close error. Acceptable for a
  benchmark; no value in surfacing it via b.Errorf since the timed
  region has already ended.
- `runBench`'s hook dispatch is a sequence of nil-checks rather than a
  loop over a slice. With three named phases this is more readable
  than a slice would be; the typed `benchHooks` struct also gives
  IDE-discoverable phase names.

### Coverage posture

The decision logic in this diff is the `runBench` wrapper (nil-check
hook dispatch, ordering of `b.ResetTimer`/`b.StopTimer` relative to
hooks). All three named benchmarks today exercise the wrapper with
`benchHooks{}`, so the empty-hook path is covered end-to-end on every
benchmark run. The non-nil-hook path is currently uncovered, which is
acceptable per option (c) — the follow-up memory/reliability bead is
the first concrete consumer that will populate hooks, and integration-
testing nil-vs-non-nil dispatch separately would duplicate that
coverage. The diff itself does not introduce production code; it adds
a test-only benchmark suite plus a backwards-compatible widening.

### Verdict

**PASS** — ready for deployer's release gate.

     `bd list`)

     so each measured insert pays a realistic per-row index cost.
   All three drive the same `runBench` wrapper, which uses
   `testfixture.ForTest(b)` for per-sample database isolation (fresh
   `bd_test_<rand>` per `-count=N` sample so accumulated row state
   cannot contaminate the next sample).

   benchstat's >= 6 confidence-interval threshold). Writes

   and `randomSuffix` now take `testing.TB` so `*testing.B` can drive

```

```
BenchmarkBdReady-32     298 ns/op   3.91ms median   258 KiB/op   1708 allocs/op
BenchmarkBdList-32      390 ns/op   3.16ms median   340 KiB/op   2256 allocs/op
BenchmarkBdCreate-32   3652 ns/op   288 µs median   6.9 KiB/op    132 allocs/op
